title: "E.3.1 Divine Hiddenness"

The argument from divine hiddenness is, alongside the evidential argument from evil, one of the contemporary arguments against a perfectly loving God. The hiddenness case is not re-argued here from first principles; instead one of the book's earned results, the account of the will (§8.9), is brought to bear, settling where the dispute lands.

*What hiddenness names.* Before the argument is met on its own terms, it is worth asking what the hiddenness in question even is. The believer and the unbeliever stand before one situation, not two: the grandeur of things is manifest and inescapable, and no God is visible within it. The hiddenness-arguer takes that silence to tell against a loving God; the believer takes the awe the grandeur provokes to be a *trace* of one. They split on the verdict but share the frame — each treats the situation as evidence bearing on a hidden author behind things, a sign that either points past itself or fails to. In neither case is the awe itself what hides — it is the most present datum a person has; what hides is the *explainer* the grandeur is taken to require, whether reached by inference or, on the reformed-epistemology variant the section meets below, taken as given in the experience itself. Hiddenness is the hiddenness of a posited cause, not of a missing object. It is that shared frame (that the grandeur, or its silence, points past itself to a transcendent author) that the book's central result cancels. On the inversion the grandeur is not a pointer to a hidden source but the manifest face of the ground itself; and a ground that conditions every moment of existence, and does so necessarily (§6.1; §6.2), is the least hidden thing there is. The relocation is not foreign to the hiddenness-arguer's own trajectory: a non-personal ultimate is what Schellenberg's later ultimism names, and the inversion arguably reaches that destination by another line. Two senses of *hidden* must not be run together here: the ground is *ontologically* manifest (it conditions everything and could not fail to) even where a *personal* God remains *epistemically* unevidenced; so 'least hidden' answers the awe-as-sign construal of hiddenness without yet touching the relationship-grade-evidence construal Schellenberg presses.

The religious response errs not in registering the greatness, which is real, but in posting it to a transcendent bearer rather than to the ground whose face it already is — the awe is veridical, its address mistaken. The misaddressing is not an ad hoc charge but a predicted one: the native dispositions the section catalogues below (a hair-trigger for agency, a bent toward purpose) deliver just this overshoot from felt grandeur to an inferred *person* (Barrett 2004; Kelemen 2004). Once that overshoot is seen as the dispositions' own contribution, the awe's standing as a *sign* falls with it.

Calling the address mistaken might still leave the grandeur looking like a message that merely reached the wrong recipient; the sharper point is that its message-character was never read off the grandeur in the first place. What the dispositions supply is not a destination but the sense that there is anything there to be addressed — that the grandeur points beyond itself, that it is *for* someone, that an author stands behind it who meant it. Strip that supplement and the splendor is undiminished and real, the manifest face of the ground it always was, yet inert as evidence of a person: a sunset loses none of its magnificence when one stops reading the sky as a message. What gets demoted is not the awe but its evidential office — so the inference from grandeur to a hidden someone is not merely misrouted but unfounded, undercut at its source by the very account of why it compels.

The debunking is bounded, not general: it bites an inference only where the disposition would fire whether or not its target were there *and* the target has no standing independent of the disposition. The awe-as-sign inference meets both conditions — the agency-sense fires on the grandeur whether or not any person stands behind it, and the posited person has no access to it except that very inference. Practices the book leans on elsewhere meet neither: moral discernment is given its own account rather than left to a bare disposition, and the modal intuitions the metaphysics runs on are constitutive of the field rather than reports about something outside it that a disposition might misrepresent. A genealogy that debunked indiscriminately would be the familiar overreach of the form; this one is held to the two conditions the awe-as-sign inference alone meets here. This does not yet settle the dispute: Schellenberg's argument is pitched at the absence of relationship-grade evidence for a *personal* God, and meeting it takes the will-result below, not a change of subject. But it relocates the disagreement before that engine engages — what presents as a God declining to appear is a demand for a hidden author behind a grandeur that was never a signature.

A perfectly loving God would want each person capable of relationship with God, and not resisting it, to be in a position to enter that relationship — which requires at least that they believe God exists. The scholastic tradition itself distinguishes these as separate stages: *assensus*, holding that God exists, and *fiducia*, trusting the God one holds to exist; the second is unavailable wherever the first has not been secured. The exemplars the tradition reaches for confirm the point rather than complicate it. Hebrews 11's roll of faith runs through exactly the figures who had the least need of *assensus*: Abraham receives the promise across direct visitations (Genesis 12, 15, 18), and Moses speaks with God "face to face, as a man speaks to his friend" (Exodus 33:11) — for these, that God exists was never the open question. What Hebrews commends in them is *fiducia* exercised from an *assensus* already secured: Abraham trusting the promise-giver's character at the binding of Isaac, Moses enduring hardship "as seeing him who is invisible" (Hebrews 11:27), not enduring uncertainty about whether anyone was there at all. The paradigm case is thus one stage short of the case it is made to justify: naming both achievements "faith" does not make the non-resistant nonbeliever's task, clearing a gate the exemplars walked through already open, the same task the exemplars performed. What follows targets only the gate, not the room behind it — the argument needs only that *assensus*, the precondition any *fiducia* would require, fails to arrive for the non-resistant through no fault of their own; whether they would go on to trust is a question that, for them, never gets asked. Yet there are *non-resistant nonbelievers* (Schellenberg's later, more careful term for the inculpable nonbelief the argument turns on, Schellenberg 2007; 2015), people open to God, who would believe if the belief were available to them, and who nonetheless do not believe. A perfectly loving God would not permit that gap. So no such God exists (Schellenberg 1993).

The standard reply denies the second premise: there are no genuinely non-resistant nonbelievers. All nonbelief is at bottom culpable — a refusal, a turning-away, a suppression of what is plainly available (the Pauline charge that they "suppress the truth," Rom 1:18–20). On this reading the hidden God is exonerated: the gap is the unbeliever's doing, a fault in the will rather than a withholding by God.

The escape is a claim about the will — that unbelief is something a person *does*, a free refusal they could simply have reversed. The book's account of the will (§8.9) is the result that claim cannot survive. Will is a current's selection over the modal field it can map, and belief is not a separate lever beside that field but a feature of it: whatever an agent holds true is already an entry in the field, and inference runs only from the entries the field contains (§8.3; §8.9.5). One cannot select into the field a possibility the field does not hold. Belief is therefore not contra-causally up to the will — a person believes what their field delivers and cannot, by willing, install a conviction the field withholds or dismiss one it compels. The doxastic involuntarism (the view that belief is not under the will's direct control) that the tradition has usually had to *assert* against the demand to "just believe" (Williams 1973; Alston 1988) falls out of the present account directly. The same result reaches Pascal's wager from the other side: the counsel to *cultivate* belief by acting as if until assent follows (§5.1.11) asks the will to install a conviction its field does not yet hold — the one thing §8.9 denies it can do.

The culpable-unbelief escape names nothing. If belief is not a contra-causal act, then "culpable unbelief" (unbelief as a free refusal the unbeliever could have reversed at will) picks out no available act. A field that does not deliver belief in God is not a will withholding assent; it is a map without that possibility. The escape requires precisely the field-independent volition the book denies: a will acting outside any modal field "acts on no possibilities… is not a free act but no act at all" (§8.9.1). Remove it, and the premise the argument needs (that non-resistant nonbelievers exist) is not merely conceded but *entailed*: wherever the field does not deliver God, the nonbelief is non-resistant by construction, because there was no resistant act there to perform.

"You could have sought" relocates the problem; it does not solve it. The fallback holds the nonbeliever responsible for not opening themselves — not seeking, not attending, not cultivating the openness that would have led to belief. But seeking is itself a selection over a field, and the same analysis governs it: one can seek with full openness and have the field still fail to deliver, and one cannot seek for a reason one's field does not yet contain. Whether the object is the belief or the seeking that might produce it, the will reaches only as far as the field reaches. The regress to "but you could have wanted to seek" terminates where every such regress does — a current does not author the field it selects within.

The deepest form of the escape (that belief is the field's default) fails on its own. The suppression charge bites only if the truth was *plainly available* to begin with: belief in God as the natural state of a properly functioning mind, so that its absence must be a defect rather than a deprivation (the reformed-epistemology backstop — the *sensus divinitatis*, Plantinga 2000). That premise breaks twice over. Structurally it is the very thing the account denies: no possibility sits in a field by default, since what a field holds is fixed by the encounters that shaped it (§8.3), not by a uniform endowment every mind carries — and "plainly available" only reinstates the field-independent deliverance §8.9.1 has already ruled out. The structural break settles it; the empirical record only corroborates. Were determinate belief in God the native default, its content would not track birthplace and century as closely as it does (Maitzen 2006), and the dispositions that do look native (a hair-trigger for agency, a bent toward purpose) yield promiscuous supernatural attribution, gods and ancestors and omens, rather than the determinate God the escape requires (Barrett 2004; Kelemen 2004). That a defender may answer that the faculty was only ever meant to seed a general sense of the divine which culture then completes does not rescue the escape: a sense culture must complete is not the field-default deliverance the suppression charge needed — it concedes the content is not native after all, relocating the unauthored-field problem rather than dissolving it. The further retreat that the faculty is real but merely *damaged* relocates it the same way: whether one's faculty is intact or damaged is itself unauthored, one more feature of the field a current did not lay down. Nor is the variance only a matter of intact against damaged. The same dispositions the defender invokes are not uniform across minds either: like any cognitive disposition they vary in strength from person to person — agency-detection running hot in some and quiet in others, the pull toward purpose stronger here and fainter there, with no pathology to mark the difference and nothing the bearer chose. A mind built toward the systematizing end is not refusing a sign; the same grandeur arrives at a receiver tuned to register it less. The faculty meant to make God plain to all is, by the lights of the case made for it, distributed unevenly along an axis no one selects. That leaves the escape a fork with no safe tine: either the faculty is the access mechanism, and a loving God has graded that mechanism and faulted those issued its shallow end (the birthplace injustice moved inward from the map to the skull), or the faculty is too uneven to carry the claim that everyone already knows, and the suppression charge has no purchase on a mind built not to see.

The asymmetry cuts both ways. If the faculty's uneven distribution makes fault an injustice for those it left blunt, the same distribution makes credit an accident for those it left sharp: a mind wired to register the pull toward purpose hotly no more earned that sensitivity than the muted mind earned its quiet. Whatever ledger the tradition would keep — desert for the believer's ready assent, fault for the unbeliever's absence of it — is drawn on an axis nobody selects, and it cannot discriminate credit from blame without discriminating on grounds neither party chose. The believer's ease is not evidence of virtue any more than the unbeliever's difficulty is evidence of vice; both report only where a given mind sat on a distribution laid down before either could have anything to say about it.

Non-resistant nonbelief, then, is not a mind malfunctioning against its own default; it is what an unpersuaded field looks like from inside.

The two engines meet here. The Chapter 6 result closes the other exit. Where the will-account removes the *culpable-unbelief* escape, the excursus's foreclosure of the appeal to mystery removes the *skeptical-theist* escape — the appeal to reasons-beyond-us that a loving God might have for remaining hidden. That retreat the excursus has already closed in general, on the voided transcendent God (§6.1, §6.2) and the symmetry that a skepticism wide enough to block the inference from evil blocks every favorable inference too; the hiddenness case inherits the result rather than re-deriving it. With no inscrutable God to ground them, "God may have reasons we cannot see" has nothing to stand on. The argument is thus pressed from both sides at once: the unbeliever's will cannot be blamed for the gap, and the hidden God cannot be excused by mystery.

A further reply grants both closures and shifts to different ground: that some measure of hiddenness is required to preserve the freedom of the response itself — an unambiguous, overwhelming God would coerce assent rather than invite it, so distance is not a defect but the condition of a genuinely free relationship (the epistemic-distance theodicy, Hick 1966). The tradition's own angelology supplies a direct counterinstance rather than a hypothetical one. Angels are held to have had access to God categorically closer than any human's — a direct, non-discursive knowledge exceeding what faith ever supplies (Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I.62) — and a third of them are reported to have rejected God regardless (Revelation 12:4). If access that close does not foreclose free rejection there, distance was never the precondition of free response the defense needs it to be; the escape trades on a claim its own tradition's angelology falsifies. The gap between what angels exercise (fiducia, freely refused despite certainty) and what the defense is pitched at protecting (assensus, belief itself) does not save it: on the will-account just established, assensus is no more a contra-causal lever than fiducia is, since both are field-governed selections rather than acts a faculty of freedom could specially guard for one and withhold from the other. If direct knowledge leaves the angels' freedom to select intact at the fiducia stage, nothing in the defense's own terms explains why the same directness would need to compromise it at the assensus stage instead.

One boundary is worth marking: this verdict stands on the book's account of the will, not on Chapters 1–5 alone. A reader who granted everything through Chapter 6 but still held belief to be a contra-causal act could refuse the conclusion — the hiddenness result binds within the §8.9 register, and there it is decisive. That register has since been strengthened: §8.9.1 now argues contra-causal volition not merely absent but incoherent (pressed for its content it resolves into determination or luck), so the holdout who insists belief is a contra-causal act is not appealing to an untouched possibility but to one the will-account argues there is no coherent room for. The refusal is available only at that contested frontier, not on the near side of it.

*What falls.* The hidden God is not exonerated by the sinner's refusal, because on the book's account there is no refusal of the needed kind — belief is not a switch the will throws. Non-resistant nonbelief is not a rare case the theist may hope away; it is what nonbelief over an unpersuaded field always is. What remains is the original problem with its best escape gone: a God said to want every open heart in relationship, and a world full of open hearts the relationship never reached.
